threads.thread_goal: Align on current move process and main problems to fix

messages.text: Kicking off the Standardised Warehouse Move and Loading Efficiency Program channel. For this first thread, can we line up how we currently run a typical move and loading shift so I can complete T1 and start shaping the incident log for A3 later on. From what I see on day shift outbound: paperwork printed, pallets staged, then loading, but I know each of you does it a bit differently. Can you walk through, step by step, how your usual inbound and outbound shifts run now, including where you see delays, confusion, or safety close calls.

For outbound day shift with mixed pallets, rough flow is: 1) I get the load sheet from the office, 2) check forklift quickly, 3) start pulling pallets from the staging area, 4) load truck based on what looks heaviest to lightest, 5) strap and close up. Pain points: sometimes the staging is not in truck order so I drive back and forth a lot, and we do not always know about fragile or dangerous goods until we see the labels. Also, when inbound trucks arrive late, we rush and skip some checks.

From my side on inbound: 1) I get told which dock to prep, 2) quick sweep and clear the area, 3) open truck and start unloading with pallet jack or crane if needed, 4) put pallets wherever there is space, 5) someone later moves them to the right zone. Delays: we often wait for clear instructions on where to place goods, and sometimes we only find out about weight limits when the mover says the pallet is too heavy for the forklift. Safety wise, the main issue is people walking through the unloading area while we are working.

Adding to what 54508 said for inbound: when we unload, we do not have a standard order. Some drivers want us to clear the back first, others the side, so we adapt each time. That makes it hard to keep a consistent flow. For outbound, when I help stage pallets, I usually: 1) check labels for destination and any hazard signs, 2) group by route, 3) try to keep heavy pallets closer to the dock. The big slowdowns are: missing paperwork, last minute changes to what goes on the truck, and waiting for a free forklift.

On night shift inbound, it is a bit more improvised. We usually: 1) get a call that a truck is at the gate, 2) open the dock and start unloading, 3) put pallets in the first free space, 4) note truck plate on a scrap paper so we can match later. Problems: we do not always know if goods need special handling, and sometimes we block aisles because we just need to get the truck out. When there is only one mover on, we wait a lot for the forklift to come back.

Thanks, this helps for T1. To make sure I capture the pain points correctly: 1) staging not matching truck order, 2) lack of clear marking for fragile and dangerous goods, 3) skipped checks when inbound is late. Anything else on outbound that really hurts time or safety, like reloading due to wrong weight distribution or incidents that should go into A3 once we start logging.

Yes, reloading happens when we realise too late that heavy pallets are all at the back or on one side. Then we have to pull some out and reshuffle. Also, sometimes we only find out a pallet is missing when the driver checks the list, so we rush to find it. For safety, the main thing is people walking behind the forklift when I am backing out of the truck.

I would add that we do not have a clear rule on who checks PPE and equipment before the shift. Sometimes I do it, sometimes the mover, sometimes no one. That leads to small issues like low battery on pallet jacks or missing straps, which slow us down. If we are going to build A3 properly, we should log those as minor delays too, not just big incidents.

On the inbound side, another issue is that we sometimes mix goods that should not be together, like food items next to chemicals, just because we are trying to clear the truck fast. Later we have to move them again to comply with hygiene rules. That is extra handling and more forklift trips.

So far I am hearing a few clusters: 1) flow and layout issues (staging order, pallets placed wherever there is space, blocked aisles), 2) information gaps (special handling, missing paperwork, last minute changes), 3) safety and checks (people in the loading zone, skipped equipment checks, mixing incompatible goods). For T1 I will write these up as the main problem areas unless anyone thinks something more critical is missing.

That grouping makes sense to me. If we have to pick what the new procedures fix first, I would prioritise: 1) clear loading and staging order so we stop reloading and extra trips, 2) standard pre-move checks so we do not skip PPE and equipment, 3) better marking and handling rules for fragile and dangerous goods. The information gaps and layout problems are what cause most of the rework I see.

I agree with those three. If we fix loading order and checks, my shift will already run smoother. The marking for fragile and dangerous goods is also key, because right now I have to stop and double check labels on the spot.

From inbound, I am ok with those as the top three. The staging order and clear rules for where to put what will help us a lot too. We can still improve other things later, but these feel like the main ones.
Same here on night shift. If we know the order and have a simple check before starting, it will reduce the rush mistakes.

Ok, I will lock in those three focus areas for the new procedures: 1) standard loading and staging order, 2) standard pre-move safety and equipment checks, 3) clear handling rules and marking for fragile and dangerous goods. I will reflect that in the T1 summary and later in A3 categories so we can track incidents and delays against them.

Next, we need to agree which typical shift we use as the reference flow for mapping and later SOPs. My suggestion is outbound day shift with mixed pallets and containers, since that is where we see most rework and it touches both staging and loading. We can still note inbound and night specifics, but the main diagram would follow that flow. Does that work, or is there a better candidate.

Outbound day shift with mixed pallets sounds right to me. That is when we have the most variety of cargo and the tightest dispatch times. If we can make that flow solid, the simpler shifts will be easier to handle.

I support using outbound day with mixed cargo as the reference. It includes staging, checks, loading, and handover to the driver, so we can build a full end to end picture. We can add short notes for inbound and night variations later in the SOP.
Works for me too. I will just make sure we flag any inbound specific issues when we review the draft later so they do not get lost.
Agree with the others. Outbound day mixed cargo as the main flow is fine. Night shift can follow the same steps with a smaller crew.

Great, I will document outbound day shift with mixed pallets and containers as our reference flow for T1 and future SOP drafts. I will post a short summary of the current steps and the three main problem areas in this channel once I have it written up, and we can use that as the base for the standard loading sequence and checks.

threads.thread_goal: Draft and refine the standard loading sequence and safety checks

messages.text: I have put together a first draft for the standard loading sequence for T2 based on our outbound day mixed cargo shift. Before we lock anything, I want your comments. Draft steps: 1) review load sheet and mark fragile and dangerous goods, 2) confirm equipment capacity and limits, 3) stage pallets in loading order, 4) load heavy and stable pallets first, 5) load medium weight and mixed pallets, 6) load fragile and light pallets last, 7) secure with straps and check weight distribution, 8) final walk around and sign off. This will later feed into A1 and link with the pre-move checklist in A2. What looks off or missing.

Thanks for writing this up. A couple of points: between steps 2 and 3, we should add a clear pre-move safety check that matches T3 and A2: PPE, equipment condition, and area clearance. Also, for step 4, we might want to specify that heavy pallets go against the headboard and over the axles where possible, not just heavy first. That will help avoid reloading due to bad weight distribution.

From the floor side, I like the structure. For staging in step 3, can we be explicit that pallets should be grouped by route and stop order, not just by cargo type. That will help us when we are preparing pallets before the truck arrives. Also, we should mention where to place goods that cannot be stacked, so we do not end up with tall unstable stacks.

I am a bit unsure about how detailed we need to be on dangerous goods in this sequence. Should we say something like: check if any pallet has hazard labels and follow the separate dangerous goods guide, or do we list exact positions here. I do not want to write something that conflicts with safety rules.

Good call. For dangerous goods, we should keep the loading sequence high level and refer to the specific safety rules instead of inventing positions. In A1 we can say: identify any dangerous goods, then follow the existing dangerous goods handling guideline and legal requirements. I will check with the health and safety officer before we finalise that part so we do not overstep.

Makes sense. So updated sequence would be: 1) review load sheet and mark fragile and dangerous goods, 2) confirm equipment capacity and limits, 3) run pre-move safety check (PPE, equipment, area) using A2 from T3, 4) stage pallets in loading order by route and stop, 5) load heavy stable pallets against headboard and over axles, 6) load medium and mixed pallets, 7) load fragile and light pallets last, 8) secure with straps and check weight distribution, 9) final walk around and sign off. Anything else we should add before we call this version 1 for the sequence.

I would add one more detail to step 8: check that straps, chains, or nets are tensioned correctly and that there is no loose cargo that can shift. Also, for fragile items, we should mention using corner protectors or padding where available. That will tie in nicely with A4 when we build the visual guide.

For the pre-move safety check in step 3, can we list the must do items that always apply, and leave optional ones for special cases. I suggest must do: PPE on, forklift and pallet jack visual check, horns and brakes tested, area around dock cleared, chocks in place if needed. Optional: extra checks for cranes or special loads.

I like that list. It is short enough to remember. Maybe we should also include a quick check that the path from staging to the dock is clear, not just the dock area itself. We often have pallets or bins in the way.

So for the always required safety checks before loading starts, we have: PPE on, equipment visual check and basic function test, dock and path cleared, wheel chocks or equivalent in place where needed. I will put these as the mandatory items in A2 and T3, and we can keep crane or special load checks as add ons. Are we all ok to treat these as non negotiable steps.
Yes, I am comfortable with those as must do checks. They are simple, cover the main risks, and fit on a one page checklist.
Agreed. If we keep it to those four mandatory checks, it will be realistic to do them every time, even when we are busy.
Works for me as well. I will use that list when I help test the checklist on shift.
I am ok with those being mandatory. It will also make it easier to explain to new crew what they must do before touching the forklift.

Taking all feedback, here is the cleaned up loading sequence I propose we use for version 1.0 in A1: 1) review load sheet and mark fragile and dangerous goods, 2) confirm equipment capacity and limits, 3) run pre-move safety check using A2 (PPE, equipment, dock and path clear, chocks as needed), 4) stage pallets in loading order by route and stop, 5) load heavy stable pallets against headboard and over axles, 6) load medium and mixed pallets, 7) load fragile and light pallets last with padding or corner protectors, 8) secure cargo with straps, chains, or nets and check for loose items, 9) final walk around and sign off. Can we agree this is the sequence we will take into the SOP and pilot.
This sequence looks solid to me and covers the main risks we discussed. I am fine using it as the base for version 1.0 and for the pilot.
I agree as well. It is clear enough that we can follow it on the floor without needing a long manual.
Looks good from my side. I will try it on my next outbound shift and note any issues for the pilot.
Ok, we will treat this nine step sequence as the standard for version 1.0 in A1 and for the pilot. I will update the draft SOP and share it back here before we brief the crew.

threads.thread_goal: Plan and confirm the pilot shift for the new procedures

messages.text: Time to set up the pilot for the new loading sequence and safety checks. Proposal: we run the pilot on next Tuesday outbound day shift, mixed pallets and containers, using the nine step sequence from A1 and the pre-move checklist from A2. For T6, we need to confirm date, time, and who is on the crew, and agree what data we will capture in A3 during the pilot. Suggested crew: 36844 as main mover, 81581 and 54508 on staging and checks, plus supervisor oversight. Does that timing and crew work, and what concerns do you see.

Tuesday outbound day works for me. That is usually a busy but not crazy day, so we can still test properly. I am ok being main mover. Only concern is if we get an extra last minute truck, we might struggle to follow every step unless the supervisor helps protect the time.

I can do Tuesday day shift and support staging and checks. To reduce the risk of skipping steps, we should agree that during the pilot we prioritise following the sequence and checklist, even if it means a small delay, so we can see the real impact. We can flag that to the supervisor and logistics planner ahead of time.

Tuesday works for me as well. I can focus on running the pre-move checklist and helping with staging in the right order. If we are logging into A3, it would help to have a simple code for each type of issue so we do not spend too long writing during the shift.

I am on night shift that week, so I will not be in the pilot crew, but I would like to see the results so we can adapt for nights later. Please make sure we capture any comments about how realistic the steps are when the dock is busy.

On the data side for A3 during the pilot, I suggest we capture at least: start and end time for the move, any incidents or near misses, any delays over five minutes and the reason, any steps that were skipped or changed and why. We can add simple codes like D for delay, I for incident, S for skipped step, plus a short note. Does that feel manageable while working.

Yes, that is manageable. We can assign one person, probably me or 54508, to jot down the codes and notes while the mover focuses on the loading. We should also capture quick feedback from the driver at the end about how the loading felt from their side.
I am ok with those data points. Maybe we also note if we had to reload anything due to weight or order issues, since that is one of our main problems.

I can take the main note taking role for A3 during the pilot. I will use the codes you suggested and add a short line for each event. We just need a printed copy of the log or a simple sheet at the dock.

On timing, can we pin down the exact window. I propose we treat the pilot as the first outbound truck on Tuesday day shift, planned for 9:00 to 11:00. That gives us time at the start of shift to brief the crew on A1 and A2, and a short debrief after. Any objections to that slot.
No objection from me. First outbound truck 9:00 to 11:00 works. I will plan to be at the dock a bit earlier to run through the checklist.
That slot is fine. I will be there from shift start so we can do a quick briefing and set up the checklist and A3 log at the dock.
Works for me too. I will handle the log and help with staging.

Ok, so pilot details are: Tuesday outbound day shift, first truck, 9:00 to 11:00, crew is 36844 as mover, 81581 and 54508 on staging and checks, supervisor informed. I will confirm this with the supervisor and logistics planner so they protect that window.

To summarise what we will capture during the pilot in A3: 1) start and end time of the move, 2) any incidents or near misses, 3) any delays over five minutes with reason, 4) any steps skipped or changed and why, 5) any reloads due to weight or order, 6) quick feedback from crew and driver on how the sequence and checklist felt. We will use simple codes D, I, S, R plus a short note. Are we all aligned on this list.
Yes, that covers what we need to judge if the new process is working. I will help make sure we actually log each event during the pilot.
Aligned. I will prepare a simple printed sheet with those codes so we can tick and write notes quickly.
Looks good to me. The reload and skipped step notes will be especially useful.
Great, we have a confirmed pilot slot and a clear list of data and feedback to capture in A3. I will share a short briefing note before Tuesday so everyone knows their role and what to watch for.

threads.thread_goal: Review pilot results and finalise SOP and guides

messages.text: Pilot summary from today for T6: we ran the new loading sequence from A1 and the pre-move checklist from A2 on the first outbound truck, mixed pallets. Times: started at 9:05, finished loading and securing at 10:02. In A3 we logged two delays (D), one reload (R) due to a heavy pallet placed too far back, and no incidents (I). We followed all nine steps, but we did rush a bit on staging. Overall, the flow felt more organised, but staging order and driver paperwork still caused some waiting.

Adding from the log in A3: Delay 1 was five minutes waiting for final paperwork from the office, Delay 2 was about seven minutes to restage two pallets when we realised the route order had changed. The reload was one heavy pallet we had to move closer to the headboard after checking weight distribution. No near misses, and the driver said the load looked more even than usual.

From my side, the pre-move checklist from A2 worked well. We did PPE, equipment checks, and cleared the dock and path before starting. That took about four minutes and did not feel like a burden. The only thing that slowed us was double checking the route order for staging. I think we should add a small note in the SOP to confirm route order with the office before staging starts.

Reading the notes in A3, it seems the new sequence helped avoid last minute surprises, even though you still had to restage. For nights, I think the checklist will be especially useful when there are fewer people around. We just need to make sure the steps fit on one page and are easy to read in low light.

Thanks for the detailed notes. For T7, I will update A1 with: 1) a clearer instruction to confirm route order before staging, 2) a reminder to check heavy pallets against headboard and axles before loading the rest, 3) a short note that paperwork delays should be logged in A3 but not lead to skipping safety checks. Before we approve version 1.0, is there anything in the sequence or checklist that felt unworkable or confusing.

Nothing felt unworkable. The only part that might need a tweak is how we phrase the staging step. Maybe say: stage pallets in loading order by route and stop, and confirm any changes with the office before moving pallets. That way we do not move them twice.

For the checklist, I suggest we keep the must do items as we tested them. They were easy to tick off. Maybe we can add a small box at the bottom for notes, so we can write if anything unusual happened. That will help when we review A3 and A8 later.

On the visual side, I started sketching stacking patterns for A4 during the pilot. The main patterns we used were: heavy pallets on the floor, lighter on top, no overhang, and fragile items on top or separate. I will turn those into simple diagrams and include a note about not stacking incompatible goods, like food and chemicals.
Those diagrams will help a lot for new staff. Maybe also show one wrong example with overhang or unstable stack, so people can see what to avoid.

Good idea on the notes box. I will add that to A2 and make sure the layout still fits on one page. For cleaning and reset, did you notice any issues after the move that we should capture in T10 and A6, like time to clear the dock or put equipment back.

After the pilot, it took us about ten minutes to sweep the dock, return straps and pallet jacks, and clear leftover pallets. That felt reasonable, but we should list those steps clearly so they do not get skipped on busy days. I can help write the list for T10.

I agree. Standard cleaning and reset steps should include: remove any loose wrap or debris, return equipment to charging or parking spots, clear the dock and path, and check that signage and barriers are back in place. We can add time estimates per area so people know what is expected.
From the mover side, I just need to remember to lower forks, park the forklift in the right spot, and note any issues before leaving the dock. If we put that in A6, it will be clear.

Based on the pilot and your inputs, I will now update A1, A2, A4, and A6 and mark them as version 1.0 for this program. Unless anyone has a strong objection, I propose we approve these as the standard for rollout to all outbound day shifts first, then extend to other shifts after a short period of use.
I support approving version 1.0 based on this pilot. The changes we discussed are small adjustments, not big redesigns, and the process already feels safer and more consistent.
Agreed. I am comfortable using these documents as the standard on my shifts. If we spot new issues, we can log them in A3 and adjust later.
I am ok with rolling out version 1.0 as well. The checklist and visual guide will make it easier to train others.
From the night shift perspective, I am fine with approving these as long as we keep an eye on how they work with smaller crews. We can feed back any night specific issues into A3 and future updates.

Ok, we will treat A1, A2, A4, and A6 as SOP and guide version 1.0 for outbound day shifts, with other shifts to follow once we have a bit more data. I will mark the documents accordingly and share the links in the channel.

Before full rollout, are there any immediate changes we should make based on the pilot, beyond the small wording tweaks we already listed. For example, do we need to change crew roles, add extra time in the schedule, or adjust cleaning steps, or can we go ahead as is and rely on the weekly reviews to catch further improvements.

I do not think we need big changes before rollout. The main immediate tweak I would suggest is to clearly assign who runs the checklist at the start of each shift, so it does not get forgotten. We can also remind everyone that cleaning and reset is part of the move, not optional.
Agree. No need to change crew size or schedule right now. If we just make sure roles are clear and we keep logging in A3, we can adjust later if we see consistent delays.
Same view here. Let us roll out with the current setup and use the weekly review notes in A8 to decide on any bigger changes later.
I am ok with that. Clear role assignment and regular reviews should be enough for now.

Understood. We will roll out version 1.0 as is, with clearer role assignment for the checklist and a reminder that cleaning and reset steps in A6 are part of the standard move. Any further changes will come from what we see in A3 and the weekly review notes in A8.

threads.thread_goal: Set up ongoing routines for training and weekly reviews

messages.text: Now that version 1.0 of the SOP and guides is ready, we need to set up training and weekly reviews. For T11 and T9, here is a proposal: 1) short on shift briefings using A7 at the start of each shift for three days, covering the new loading sequence, checklist A2, visual guide A4, and cleaning steps A6; 2) a weekly 20 minute review using A3 and A8 to look at incidents, delays, and feedback. I suggest we do the weekly review every Wednesday at 14:00 so both day and night leads can feed in. Thoughts on timing and how we collect incidents and feedback before each review.

For the briefings, I suggest we keep them to 10 minutes max and focus on three key points per session: day one on the loading sequence, day two on the checklist, day three on stacking and cleaning. That will make it easier to fit into shift handover. I can help run the first couple of briefings on day shift.

Wednesday 14:00 for the weekly review works for me most weeks, as long as we keep it tight. For collecting incidents and feedback, I think we should ask movers and factory hands to jot things down in A3 during the week, and then maybe send a quick note in this channel before the review if there is something urgent.

I like the idea of short briefings. For night shift, we might need a different time, maybe at the start of their shift. On incident collection, could we have a simple rule that any delay over five minutes or any safety concern gets logged in A3, even if it feels small.

For nights, a quick briefing at shift start is fine. I can help explain the checklist and cleaning steps. On the weekly review time, I will not be there in person, but I can leave notes in A3 and maybe a short summary in the channel before Wednesday.

So for the weekly review routine in T9, we could define it as: every Wednesday 14:00, 20 minutes, using A3 and A8, with at least one mover and one factory hand present or sending notes. Agenda: top three issues from the log, actions and owners, quick check if any SOP or checklist change is needed. Are you ok to lock that in as the standard slot.
Yes, that works. If someone cannot attend, they can still add their points to A3 or A8 beforehand.
Agreed on Wednesday 14:00 as the review time and the agenda you described.
Fine by me. I will make sure we have the latest A3 entries ready before the meeting.
I am ok with that slot. I will just send my notes ahead of time since I will be on nights.
Great, Wednesday 14:00 is now our standard weekly review time. I will set up a recurring reminder and a simple A8 template for notes and actions.

On training content for T11, I plan to cover: 1) key steps from the SOP A1, 2) how to use the checklist A2, 3) main stacking and securing patterns from A4, 4) cleaning and reset steps from A6, 5) how and when to log in A3. Briefings will be at shift start for three days in a row for each shift. Does that cover the main topics, or is there anything else we should add.
That list looks complete. Maybe just emphasise in the briefings that people should speak up if a step feels unclear or hard to follow, so we can adjust later instead of quietly skipping it.
I would also mention who is responsible for each part: who runs the checklist, who leads loading, who signs off cleaning. That will help avoid confusion during shifts.

For collecting feedback for T12, maybe at the end of each briefing we can ask two quick questions: did this make your work easier or harder, and do you feel safer with these steps. We can note answers and later summarise them.
I like that. On nights, I can ask the same two questions and send the answers here so they get included in T12.

Good point. For T12, we will collect at least three crew feedbacks by asking those two questions during briefings and logging short answers. We can then summarise into a few key points and link them to what we see in A3.

To make it clear how incidents and feedback will be collected before each weekly review, I propose: 1) all delays over five minutes, any safety concerns, and any reloads are logged in A3 during the week; 2) before Wednesday 14:00, each shift lead checks the log and adds any extra comments; 3) if there is something urgent, they post a short note in this channel so we do not wait for the review. Are we ok to treat this as our standard collection method.
Yes, that is clear and practical. It should give us enough information for the weekly review without adding too much admin.
Agreed. I will make sure to log delays and reloads in A3 and flag anything urgent here.
Works for me. I will help keep the log up to date on my shifts.
I am ok with that approach as well. I will add night shift notes into A3 and here before the review.

Great, so we have a fixed weekly review time and a clear way to collect incidents and feedback. I will finalise A7 with the briefing plan and update A8 with the review template, then share both so we can start next week.
